strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing proactive interference with clear cognitive psychology parallels
Principled tool design with four sound design principles leading to practical, implementable tools
Valuable empirical insights in Section 4.1 analyzing why unguided tool use fails, providing clear guidance for future work
Strong experimental results on key benchmarks: +27 pts on NeedleBench, +73% on 5-needle tasks, 81.4% context reduction
Novel RL training approach with conditional trajectory collection and incremental loss assignment that elegantly handles non-monotonic context evolution
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple models (Claude-4-Sonnet, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3, M3) and diverse benchmarks
Solid value-specific attention analysis with 93.5% of pairs showing improved attention allocation when using folding
Excellent reproducibility documentation with detailed hyperparameters, training configurations, and complete tool schemas in appendix
weaknesses: Zero-shot performance heavily depends on hand-crafted benchmark-specific prompts, limiting practical applicability; suboptimal guidance shows models struggle (72% vs 89.9%)
Weak baseline comparisons: RAG uses only BM25 without dense embeddings; missing comparisons to LLMLingua and modern retrieval systems; MemAgent on different foundations
Inconsistent results across models: DeepSeek-V3 shows -0.12 average on PI-LLM, indicating non-universal applicability; minimal investigation into failure cases
Poor performance on reasoning-heavy tasks: LongBenchV2 (+1.5 pts, still 34.5%) and FRAMES (-0.6 pts, decreased); suggests scope limited to retrieval rather than complex reasoning
Limited generalization: RL training on simple benchmarks (BABILong, GSM-Infinite) shows modest transfer to complex benchmarks, with no evidence of cross-domain generalization
Moderate attention improvements: mean 9.87% with 6.5% negative cases and high variance; statistically significant but not dramatic
Low tool design novelty: fragmentation, folding, and search are straightforward; primary contribution is application rather than methodology
Arbitrary experimental choices without justification: 20-tool budget, training dataset selection, simplistic reward design lacking sensitivity analysis
Significant reproducibility barriers: M3 requires 128 H800 GPU pre-training; code/data release not mentioned; results limited to text-only long-context tasks
